criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Memo identifies ELUR conflict with ground-floor residential use
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the conflict in Issue 6, titled 'The ELUR Prohibits Ground-Floor Residential Use and the Project Program Assumes It.' It quotes the ELUR's prohibition on 'residential use' on the ground floor (including habitable space for residential dwelling, sleeping, cooking, or eating), contrasts it with the Term Sheet's description of 'ground-floor residential lobby and amenity spaces (fitness center, package room, resident lounge, and leasing office),' notes the Phase II ESA's interpretive ambiguity and enforcement exposure, and references the recorded ELUR (Volume 412, Page 88) in Part I. It also proposes draft-lease treatment (Sections 9.3, 5.6) and fallbacks. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Lease defines permitted residential use to exclude ground-floor habitable space
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly distinguishes habitable from non-habitable ground-floor space. Section 9.3(a) prohibits constructing dwelling units on the ground floor and bars habitable residential space at or below finished grade, citing ELUR compliance. Section 9.3(b) permits non-habitable ancillary ground-floor uses (residential lobby, leasing office, package/mail room, management office, MEP rooms, parking, bicycle storage, fitness center, resident lounge). Section 9.3(d) further restricts Affordable Units to the second floor and above. Section 5.6(b) acknowledges the ELUR interpretive ambiguity for ancillary spaces and Section 5.6(d)/9.3(c) provide DEEP-determination remedies. This satisfies the criterion, which permits either distinguishing habitable vs. non-habitable spaces or restricting dwelling units to upper floors—the lease does both.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Affordable housing units specified for upper floors only
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease explicitly addresses this. Section 9.3(d) states: "Affordable dwelling units shall be located exclusively on the second floor and above, in accordance with the recommendation of Halcyon Environmental Consultants Inc. in the Phase II Environmental Site Assessment." This is reinforced by Section 9.3(a) (no dwelling units on ground floor, no habitable residential space at/below grade, in compliance with the ELUR) and Exhibit G, Item 4 ("Affordable Units shall be located on the second floor and above (Section 9.3(d))"). The lease thus expressly ties upper-floor placement of the 15%/80% AMI affordable units to the ELUR ground-floor residential restriction.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Memo identifies mechanics' lien as title defect requiring resolution
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the mechanics' lien in Issue 7 ('The Mechanics' Lien Is Being Passed to You as a Permitted Exception'), stating that Calloway Marine Demolition Inc. filed a $187,500 mechanics' lien on April 3, 2025 at Volume 418, Page 302, that Title Commitment Requirement No. 7 bars issuance of either policy until it is satisfied, and that the Draft Lease requires the Authority to discharge, bond, or insure over the lien before the Lease Commencement Date. The lien is also listed in the Executive Summary (Rank 9) and the Complete Issue Log (item 4), so it is clearly identified as a title defect requiring resolution.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Lease requires Authority to discharge mechanics' lien as condition precedent or provides indemnity
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly places the burden of clearing the Calloway Marine Demolition mechanics' lien on the Authority. Section 2.6(a)(v) makes discharge, bonding, or other disposition of the lien (so that it is not a Permitted Exception) a condition precedent to the Lease Commencement Date. Section 17.1(g) is an express Landlord representation/covenant that the Authority shall, at its sole cost, discharge or bond off the lien under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37 (or have it insured over) before the Lease Commencement Date, and states Tenant is not responsible for the amount. Exhibit I, item 6 confirms the lien is NOT a Permitted Exception and must be cleared by Landlord at its sole cost. This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Memo identifies rent calculation rounding discrepancy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo does not flag the specified rounding discrepancy. It states in Part V that $2,850,000 ÷ 139,392 SF = $20.4459/SF and marks it 'Reconciled,' but it never identifies that $20.45/SF × 139,392 SF yields approximately $2,850,566, nor does it discuss the resulting ~$566 discrepancy or which figure controls. Therefore it fails the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Lease specifies which rent figure controls (lump sum vs. per-SF rate)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.1 states the controlling annual Base Rent as $2,850,000 and describes the $20.45 per square foot figure as 'approximately,' satisfying the criterion that the per-SF rate be identified as approximate/illustrative.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Memo identifies conflict between reverter right and lender security interest
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly and repeatedly identifies this conflict. Issue 3, titled 'The Reverter Cannot Be Reconciled With the Leasehold Mortgage as Drafted,' carries a Critical severity rating and details how the Term Sheet's automatic termination and New Lease right (limited to Tenant default, with cure periods running from termination) conflict with Bayside's Sections 5.3, 5.4, 5.5, and 5.7, noting these are conditions precedent to loan closing under Bayside Section 6(a). It states the automatic termination feature 'makes the New Lease right largely illusory: a lender cannot elect a new lease if the lease has already terminated and the improvements have vested in the fee owner free of its claims.' The Executive Summary risk register also flags the reverter as an 'uninsurable lender objection' incompatible with the $285M leasehold mortgage, and Issue 2 notes it is 'an obstacle no construction lender will underwrite.' The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Lease subordinates reverter right to leasehold mortgage/lender protections
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains extensive lender protections against the reverter right. Section 7.6(c) requires simultaneous notice to each Leasehold Mortgagee and an independent 180-day cure period, during which the lender may cure by performing the Milestone, advancing funds, or installing a replacement developer. Section 7.6(d) provides that the reverter is of no effect if the Mortgagee exercises its New Lease right under Section 10.4. Section 7.6(e) expressly subordinates the reverter right to each Leasehold Mortgage. Section 10.2 requires delivery of Milestone Notices to lenders, Section 10.3(c) grants the 180-day milestone cure period, and Section 10.4 gives the lender a New Lease right even upon a Reverter Termination. These provisions fully satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Memo identifies conflict between ROFR and lender foreclosure rights
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies this conflict. Issue 8, titled 'The Recorded Right of First Refusal Does Not Contemplate the Financing' (ranked Critical), states that the recorded ROFR covering 'any assignment... of the leasehold interest' can be read to capture the granting of the leasehold mortgage (colliding with Bayside Section 5.1's requirement of no consent) and that foreclosure sale transfers or deeds-in-lieu would trigger the ROFR, colliding with Bayside Section 5.6's requirement of no landlord consent for foreclosure and assignment. It also notes the ROFR lacks mortgage/foreclosure carve-outs, and proposes Section 11.6 carve-outs plus a recorded amendment as a closing condition. The issue log (Item 5) reinforces this.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Lease carves out lender foreclosure/transfers from ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly carves out lender foreclosure and related transfers from the Authority's right of first refusal. Section 11.6(a) provides that the ROFR does not apply to '(i) the grant, amendment, renewal, replacement, enforcement, or foreclosure of any Leasehold Mortgage' or '(ii) any Transfer by a Leasehold Mortgagee or its designee under Section 10.6, including any assignment following foreclosure or deed in lieu,' along with Permitted Transfers, subleases, and equity transfers. Section 11.3(b) and (c) similarly treat pledges to and foreclosures by a Leasehold Mortgagee as Permitted Transfers that do not trigger the ROFR, and Section 10.6(c) confirms no foreclosure/deed-in-lieu transfer constitutes a Transfer or triggers the ROFR. Section 11.6(b)-(c) further requires amending the recorded ROFR Declaration to implement these carve-outs and subordinate it to the Leasehold Mortgages, with recording as a condition to Lease Commencement. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo identifies 12-month force majeure cap may be insufficient for coastal waterfront project
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses coastal storm risk and recommends expanding the force majeure list, but it does not identify the 12-month aggregate force majeure cap itself as potentially insufficient for a FEMA Flood Zone AE waterfront project, nor does it recommend increasing that aggregate cap beyond 12 months. Its added extensions are for ELUR/title/City delays or a discretionary 6-month extension, not a critique of the 12-month force majeure cap.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo recommends force majeure cover climate-related events
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly recommends expanding force majeure provisions to address climate-related events. In Issue 11 (and log item 40), it notes that the Term Sheet's force majeure list omits 'named storms, tidal flooding, storm surge,' and the Position Taken states that Section 7.4 expands the force majeure list to include 'named storms, tidal flooding and storm surge, FEMA map changes.' It also cites the ESA's nor'easter observations and its recommendation to calibrate force majeure to coastal storm risk. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Memo identifies CPI rent reset gap period ambiguity
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses CPI resets and notes defects such as an uncapped 'greater of' and missing base index month, but it does not identify the specific structural ambiguity described: that fixed 2.5% compounding applies for Years 1–15, CPI resets occur every 10 years beginning Year 16, and the term sheet is silent on what governs annual increases during the periods between CPI reset dates (e.g., Years 16–25). No passage flags this gap-period ambiguity.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Lease specifies interim escalation mechanism between CPI resets
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes Section 3.3, which resets Base Rent to the greater of continued 2.5% compounding or CPI on Reset Dates (Rent Years 16, 26, 36, etc.). Between resets, Exhibit B Part 1 provides a detailed schedule showing Base Rent payable in each five-year band (e.g., Rent Years 16-20 at $4,127,650, 21-25 at $4,670,057), which reflects continued 2.5% annual escalation. The schedule is incorporated into the lease and explicitly states the rent payable, satisfying the requirement for an interim escalation mechanism.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Memo identifies that percentage rent breakpoint is not indexed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the issue: Rank 6 risk and Issue 5 state that the $28,500,000 Breakpoint is 'a fixed dollar amount and shall remain unchanged for the duration of the Lease Term,' that over a 99-year term the effective participation rate rises continuously, describing the result as 'a second ground rent' or gross receipts tax (percentage rent rising from ~0.9% to ~30% of Base Rent, ~$146 million more than an indexed construct). It recommends indexing the Breakpoint in lockstep with Base Rent (Section 4.2), with a fallback of CPI-based annual indexing or periodic resets at ten-year CPI Reset Dates, and it is logged as Issue 15. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Lease indexes or periodically resets the percentage rent breakpoint
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 of the lease expressly provides a breakpoint adjustment mechanism: after Rent Year 5, the initial $28,500,000 Breakpoint is increased each Rent Year by the same cumulative percentage as Base Rent increases (with a floor of $28.5M), preserving the original 8.84x relationship to Base Rent. Section 4.2(c) requires annual written confirmation and provides for Expert determination of disputes, and Exhibit B illustrates the indexed Breakpoint over the 99-year Term (showing it rising to over $263 million by Rent Year 99). The criterion is therefore satisfied—the breakpoint is not fixed for the term but is periodically adjusted/indexed.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Memo identifies tax abatement timing misalignment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo directly flags the tax abatement timing misalignment in Issue 4, explaining that the Term Sheet starts the 15-year abatement on the Lease Commencement Date (October 1, 2025), while rent does not commence until October 1, 2028. It notes that roughly three abatement years are consumed during construction when there is no project income and that the abatement delivers almost nothing because the property is assessed as unimproved land. It also quantifies the lost value (~$4.6 million) and recommends shifting the abatement commencement to the Rent Commencement Date. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Lease specifies tax abatement commences upon Rent Commencement or first CO
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease explicitly defines the Abatement Commencement Date as the later of the Rent Commencement Date and the first day of the first Abatement Year in which the property is assessed as improved following substantial completion of Phase 1. It also expressly states no abatement period is consumed during the Rent Abatement Period or while taxes are paid on an unimproved parcel, so the abatement is tied to revenue/project completion rather than the Lease Commencement Date.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Memo addresses unconscionability of improvement forfeiture under reverter
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly addresses the reverter forfeiture as a potential penalty and disproportionate forfeiture, citing Connecticut liquidated-damages/penalty doctrine and Restatement principles on unconscionability and relief from forfeiture. It quantifies the enormous improvement forfeiture relative to the Authority's likely harm and recommends alternatives including fair market value or Net Hard Costs compensation, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Lease mitigates improvement forfeiture with buyout or reimbursement
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly mitigates forfeiture of improvements upon reverter. Article 7 (Sections 7.6–7.7) conditions any Reverter Termination on Landlord's payment of 'Reverter Compensation' equal to the greater of (i) the Fair Market Value of the Improvements (determined by MAI appraisal) or (ii) Tenant's Net Hard Costs (documented out-of-pocket hard construction costs), reduced only by limited Landlord Damages. Section 7.7(e) bars Landlord from recovering possession until the compensation is paid or escrowed, and Section 7.7(f) expressly states there is 'No forfeiture' and that Landlord is not entitled to any Improvement without payment. Section 7.8 gives Landlord an optional purchase right at the same compensation price. The lease also supersedes the Term Sheet's harsher terms (automatic termination and full security deposit forfeiture) via Sections 7.6(b) and 7.9. While Section 16.2 provides for uncompensated passing of Improvements at natural expiration of the 99-year Term, that is ordinary ground lease reversion at end of term, not a forfeiture/reverter upon default, and the reverter scenario—the subject of the criterion—is fully compensated. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Memo identifies missing estoppel certificate framework
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo does not identify the absence of an estoppel certificate framework. Estoppel is mentioned only glancingly in the Next Steps table ('confirm the lender's estoppel and SNDA requirements') and, more problematically, Part VIII's 'Items that are not applicable' section expressly states that 'there is no rent roll or estoppel exercise, because the Project has no tenants' — treating estoppel as inapplicable rather than as a critical missing framework for refinancing over a 99-year ground lease with a leasehold mortgage. The 55-item issue log contains no entry flagging that neither the Term Sheet nor the Bayside Term Sheet addresses estoppel certificate obligations, and no analysis explains why estoppel certificates matter for refinancing. The criterion is therefore not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease includes estoppel certificate provision with specified timeframe
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 18.4 of the lease contains an estoppel certificate provision that expressly obligates each party, including the Authority as Landlord, to deliver an estoppel certificate within ten (10) Business Days after request, and further provides that failure to respond binds the non-responding party to the requesting party's certified matters. This satisfies the requirement of an estoppel provision with a specified response timeframe. Section 10.1(b) also obligates Landlord to deliver estoppels to Leasehold Mortgagees upon request. The specific 10-business-day deadline meets the criterion (a specified timeframe, even if shorter than the 15-30 day example).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease estoppel provision includes deemed-approval mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 18.4 includes an express deemed-confirmation mechanism: if a party fails to deliver an estoppel certificate within 10 Business Days, the requesting party may certify the matters in its request and the non-responding party is bound. This applies to the Authority as Landlord.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Memo identifies lack of affordable housing implementation detail
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly flags the gap in affordable housing implementation details. Complete Issue Log item 38 states that the recorded affordable housing covenant omits recalculation, verification, monitoring, enforcement, and location rules, and that there are inconsistent AMI geographies. Item 54 further notes uncertainty over remedies for non-compliance. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Lease includes substantive affordable housing compliance provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 9.4 (supplemented by Exhibit G) provides substantive affordable housing implementation detail well beyond a bare restatement of the 15% requirement. It addresses (a) calculation methodology — 15% of total unit count as finally designed, rounded up, with recalculation on unit-count changes (Section 9.4(b)); (b) income verification and eligibility — affirmative marketing plan, income verification at initial occupancy and annually, annual compliance certificate with rent roll and income bands (Section 9.4(e), Exhibit G ¶¶2-6); (c) compliance monitoring/reporting mechanism (Section 9.4(e) and Exhibit G ¶9 monitoring entity conforming amendment); (d) consequences of non-compliance — notice, 60-day cure, remedies limited to specific performance/injunction, expressly no default or reverter (Section 9.4(f)); and (f) incorporation of a recorded regulatory agreement/covenant — deed restriction consistent with the Affordable Housing Restrictive Covenant at Volume 408, Page 230, with a conforming amendment required (Section 9.4(a), Exhibit G ¶9). It also fixes the AMI standard and HUD area (Section 9.4(c)) and duration for the Term. This satisfies far more than two of the enumerated elements.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Landlord name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease names the Landlord as 'CITY OF PORT CALLOWAY REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY' and describes it as 'a public body corporate and politic organized and existing under the provisions of the Connecticut General Statutes, Section 8-125 et seq.' This appears consistently in the preamble, signature block, and Memorandum of Lease, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Tenant name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease identifies the Tenant in the preamble as 'MERIDIAN GATEWAY HOLDINGS LLC, a Delaware limited liability company registered to do business in the State of Connecticut,' and Section 17.2(a) confirms it is a limited liability company duly organized under the laws of Delaware. Both the name and entity type match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct property address and APN
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease prominently identifies the property as "10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, Connecticut 06801" and "Assessor's Parcel No. 127-003-0045" in the cover block, Recital A, Section 2.2, and Exhibits A and D. Both the address and APN match the criterion exactly, and neither is materially incorrect or missing.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct parcel size
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease repeatedly and consistently states the parcel size as approximately 3.2 acres / 139,392 square feet — in Recital A ("approximately 3.2 acres (139,392 square feet)"), Section 3.1 (rent per square foot based on 139,392 square feet), Exhibit A ("Containing 139,392 square feet, or 3.200 acres... which stated area controls for all purposes"), and Memorandum of Lease ("containing 139,392 square feet (3.2 acres)"). The discrepancy with the erroneous title commitment description (279,535 sq ft) is expressly identified and resolved in favor of the correct 139,392 sq ft / 3.2 acre figure. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct lease term of 99 years from October 1, 2025
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly states a 99-year term, defines the Lease Commencement Date as October 1, 2025 (or later if conditions are not satisfied), and sets the expiration date as September 30, 2124. The required dates and 99-year term are present.

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct initial annual base rent of $2,850,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.1 states initial annual Base Rent of $2,850,000, payable in equal monthly installments of $237,500 on the first day of each calendar month. The stated per-square-foot figure (~$20.45 based on 139,392 sq ft) is also arithmetically consistent ($2,850,000 / 139,392 ≈ $20.446), and Exhibit B repeats the same amounts. Both the annual and monthly figures match the criterion exactly.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct Rent Commencement Date definition
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 2.7 correctly states the first prong (earlier of 36 months after the Lease Commencement Date), but the second prong does not match the criterion. Instead of the first certificate of occupancy 'for any portion of the Project,' the lease requires a CO covering 'Occupancy Trigger Space' (≥75% of residential units plus retail available for fit-out) and expressly provides that 'No certificate of occupancy for a nominal, incidental, or partial portion of the Project (including a sales center, leasing office, model unit, amenity space, or single retail bay) shall accelerate the Rent Commencement Date.' Because the defined trigger is narrower than, and inconsistent with, the required 'first certificate of occupancy for any portion of the project,' the Rent Commencement Date definition is incorrect under the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct fixed rent escalation: 2.5% compounding every 5 years
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.2 expressly provides that Base Rent escalates at 2.5% per annum, compounded annually, applied in five-year steps. It computes Rent Years 6–10 at $3,224,513/year (2,850,000 × 1.025^5 = 3,224,513) and Rent Years 11–15 at $3,648,241/year (2,850,000 × 1.025^10 = 3,648,241), matching the criterion's expected figures (~$3,224,500 and ~$3,648,200). Monthly installments ($268,709.42 and $304,020.08) are consistent with annual/12. Exhibit B reproduces the same schedule (with a trivial $0.03 rounding variance in one monthly figure that is immaterial). The formula is also declared controlling over any table discrepancy. All requirements of the criterion are satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes CPI rent reset mechanism starting Year 16
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.3 explicitly implements the required CPI reset: it triggers on the first day of Rent Year 16 and every tenth Rent Year thereafter (Rent Years 16, 26, 36, 46, 56, 66, 76, 86, and 96), uses the CPI-U for the Northeast Region (Series ID CUUR0100SA0) as defined in Article 1, and sets annual Base Rent at the greater of (i) the continued 2.5% compounded fixed escalation from the initial $2,850,000 Base Rent, or (ii) the initial Base Rent multiplied by the CPI ratio (CPI three months before the Reset Date over the Base Index Month). Exhibit B also reflects the reset structure for Years 16 onward. The additional Reset Cap (clause (ii) limited to 150% of the clause (i) increase) and the no-reduction floor are refinements of the greater-of mechanic rather than a departure from it, so the criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct percentage rent terms
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.1 provides Percentage Rent of exactly 2.0% of the amount by which Gross Revenues exceed the Breakpoint, commencing with Rent Year 6 and continuing for the remainder of the Term. Section 4.2(a) sets the Year 6 Breakpoint at $28,500,000 (indexed thereafter in lockstep with Base Rent, which the criterion expressly permits). Section 4.5 requires annual calculation and payment within 90 days after the end of each Rent Year, with a certified statement of Gross Revenues. Gross Revenues exclusions in Section 4.4 are conventional. All three elements—rate, commencement year, and payment timing—match the criterion. The only minor variance is measuring 'Year 6' from the Rent Commencement Date (Rent Year) rather than the Lease Commencement Date, but the lease explicitly defines and reconciles Term Year versus Rent Year, and percentage rent contemporaneous with rent obligation is standard and not a material discrepancy.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct remediation credit of $1,800,000
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes a $1,800,000 Remediation Credit in Section 5.3, applied against Base Rent beginning on the Rent Commencement Date: full credit for months 1–7 at $237,500/month ($1,662,500 total) and a partial credit of $137,500 in month 8, with full Base Rent thereafter. This matches the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit amount and form (LOC)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.1 requires a security deposit of $5,700,000 (24 months of initial monthly Base Rent). Section 8.2(a) requires the deposit to be evidenced by an irrevocable standby letter of credit substantially in the form of Exhibit F, issued by a commercial bank with a minimum long-term credit rating of A- from S&P Global Ratings or A3 from Moody's (or equivalent). Exhibit F further specifies the irrevocable standby LC terms. Amount, form, and credit rating requirements all match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit reduction mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.3 expressly provides that the Security Deposit reduces to $2,850,000 after Tenant demonstrates that the Project has achieved and maintained a 90% Occupancy Rate for 24 consecutive months. The occupancy rate is further defined, and the reduction procedure is specified, so the required mechanism is present and correct.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 1: construction commencement within 18 months (by April 1, 2027)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.3 of the lease expressly defines Milestone 1 as 'Commencement of Construction: physical pouring of footings for at least one building within the Project, following issuance of all necessary building permits,' with a period of 18 months from the Lease Commencement Date and a deadline of April 1, 2027 (based on the stated Lease Commencement Date of October 1, 2025). Exhibit C repeats the same milestone, timing, and deadline. The milestone is present, correctly scoped to construction commencement, and correctly dated within 18 months.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 2: structural frame within 42 months (by April 1, 2029)
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes Milestone 2 in Section 7.3 requiring completion of the structural frame for the Residential Tower within 42 months of the Lease Commencement Date, with an example deadline of April 1, 2029 if commencement is October 1, 2025. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 3: Phase 1 substantial completion within 60 months (by October 1, 2030)
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly includes Milestone 3 requiring Substantial Completion of Phase 1 within 60 months of the Lease Commencement Date, with an October 1, 2030 deadline if commencement is October 1, 2025. This appears in Section 7.3 and Exhibit C.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 4: Phase 2 substantial completion within 84 months (by October 1, 2032)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.3 of the lease includes a Milestone table with Milestone 4: 'Substantial Completion of Phase 2: issuance of a temporary or permanent certificate of occupancy for the Office Building,' with a period of 84 months from the Lease Commencement Date and a stated deadline of October 1, 2032 (assuming an October 1, 2025 Lease Commencement Date), which is mathematically correct. Exhibit C (Development Milestone Schedule) repeats the same Milestone 4 requirement with the same 84-month period and October 1, 2032 deadline. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes force majeure extension provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.4(a) expressly provides that each Milestone Deadline is extended day-for-day for Force Majeure, capped at an aggregate of twelve (12) months across all Milestones, plus a further extension of up to six (6) months in the aggregate for governmental permitting delays beyond Tenant's reasonable control (total 18 months). Section 7.4(b) defines Force Majeure broadly (severe weather, named storms, tidal flooding, FEMA flood map changes, governmental delays, etc.), with notice/mitigation mechanics and Expert resolution of disputes in Section 7.4(f). Exhibit C also restates the 12-month Force Majeure and 6-month permitting extension framework. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes reverter right provisions for Milestones 1 and 3
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly defines "Milestone Failure" (Section 1.1) as Tenant's failure to achieve Milestone 1 or Milestone 3 by the applicable Milestone Deadline, as extended. Article 7 contains a full reverter regime: Section 7.5 requires Landlord to deliver a Milestone Notice and gives Tenant a 180-day "Milestone Cure Period"; Section 7.6(a) permits Landlord to effect a "Reverter Termination" by written notice delivered after that 180-day cure period expires (and after Leasehold Mortgagee cure periods under Section 10.3); Section 7.7 provides compensation on reverter; Section 7.10 lists circumstances excluding reverter; Section 7.12 confirms the milestone covenants; and Exhibit C confirms that "[o]nly Milestones 1 and 3 are subject to the reverter right." Thus the reverter right for Milestones 1 and 3, tied to a 180-day written notice/cure period, is present and specified. (The lease adds lender protections and compensation mechanics, but does not omit the required 180-day notice element.)

criteria_results.title: Lease includes leasehold mortgage permission for construction financing
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly permits leasehold mortgages for construction financing. Recital E states the Project will be financed in part with a construction loan from Bayside Federal Lending Corp. secured by a first-priority leasehold mortgage on Tenant's leasehold interest and the Improvements, and that the parties intend a financeable, institutional-quality ground lease. Article 10 (Section 10.1(a)) expressly grants Tenant the right to grant one or more Leasehold Mortgages to any Qualified Mortgagee without Landlord's consent, joinder, or fee, and Article 10 further provides extensive Leasehold Mortgagee protections (notice, cure rights, New Lease rights, SNDA, foreclosure/deed-in-lieu rights). 'Leasehold Mortgage' and 'Qualified Mortgagee' are defined terms encompassing construction lenders. Therefore the criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes SNDA framework with the Authority
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly provides an SNDA framework. Section 10.7 requires Landlord (the Authority) to execute and deliver to each Leasehold Mortgagee (including Bayside, the construction lender) a Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment Agreement substantially in the form of Exhibit E, with enumerated minimum provisions (recognition of mortgage priority, non-disturbance, attornment, notice/cure, new lease rights, proceeds, no amendment without consent, etc.). Exhibit E sets forth the SNDA terms in detail, and Section 2.6(a)(i) makes execution and delivery of the SNDA a condition to the Lease Commencement Date. This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes New Lease right for lender if ground lease is terminated
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes an express New Lease right in Article 10, Section 10.4. It allows each Leasehold Mortgagee or its designee, if the ground lease is terminated for any reason including Tenant default, to obtain a new ground lease on the same terms for the remainder of the Term. The provision requires the lender to cure monetary defaults within 60 days and non-monetary defaults within 90 days, or to commence cure within 90 days and diligently pursue completion. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires Authority to provide lender copies of default notices
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.2 expressly requires the Authority (Landlord) to deliver to each Leasehold Mortgagee, simultaneously with delivery to Tenant, a copy of every notice of default, notice of termination, Milestone Notice, and other notices materially affecting Tenant's leasehold interest, and states failure to do so renders the notice ineffective. Section 15.2 reinforces this by requiring simultaneous delivery of each Tenant Event of Default notice to each Leasehold Mortgagee. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease prohibits voluntary surrender without lender consent
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.5 expressly prohibits Landlord from accepting a voluntary surrender, cancellation, or termination of the Lease without the prior written consent of the Leasehold Mortgagee while any Leasehold Mortgage remains in effect, with purported surrenders void as against the mortgagee.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes ELUR acknowledgment and compliance obligations
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly references the Environmental Land Use Restriction (ELUR) recorded at Volume 412, Page 88, including in the recitals, definitions, Article 5, and Exhibit I. It includes compliance obligations under Section 5.6, the engineered barrier requirement in Section 5.7, restrictions on ground-floor residential use and ground disturbance, annual compliance certification, and related remediation/soil management obligations. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease specifies Tenant's remaining remediation responsibility of $600,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 5.3 grants a $1,800,000 Remediation Credit against Base Rent, Section 5.4(a) states Tenant bears the estimated $2,400,000 in remediation costs, and Exhibit H, Part 2 expressly reconciles the two: estimated cost $2,400,000 less the $1,800,000 credit equals a 'Net estimated Tenant cost after credit' of $600,000. The allocation is clearly and correctly specified, matching the criterion's required figures.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes comprehensive insurance requirements
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 12 of the lease sets out comprehensive insurance obligations that satisfy every element of the criterion. Section 12.1 requires: (a) Commercial General Liability at $10,000,000 per occurrence / $20,000,000 aggregate; (b) All-Risk Property insurance on a replacement-cost basis; (c) Builder's Risk on a completed-value form during construction; (d) Flood insurance, further detailed in Section 12.4 (FEMA Zone AE, PML/maximum available coverage); (e) Environmental/Pollution Legal Liability at $5,000,000 per occurrence / $10,000,000 aggregate; and (f) Workers' Compensation at statutory limits plus employer's liability. Section 12.2(c) names the Landlord/Authority as an additional insured on the CGL, umbrella, and automobile policies and as loss payee on the property policy with respect to its fee interest. All six required coverages are present and the Authority is named on the liability and property policies (loss payee being the customary property-policy designation), so the criterion is met.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes triple-net structure for taxes and operating costs
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease functionally establishes a triple-net structure: Tenant pays all real property taxes and assessments (Article 6), maintains and repairs the Premises and Improvements (Section 9.6), pays utilities and operating costs (Sections 6.8 and 9.6), and carries the required insurance (Article 12). Rent is absolute and not subject to abatement except limited casualty/condemnation provisions. Although the lease does not use the label 'triple net,' the substantive obligations satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes tax abatement phase-in schedule
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.3(a) of the lease includes an explicit tax abatement phase-in schedule: Abatement Years 1-5 at 25% of full assessed value, Years 6-10 at 50%, Years 11-15 at 75%, and 100% (full assessment) thereafter. The table also includes estimated annual taxes and the abatement is further implemented through the Tax Abatement Agreement referenced in Section 6.3(b). This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes permitted use restrictions consistent with term sheet
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 9.1 permits residential apartments, Class A office, ground-floor retail, restaurants including liquor service, and accessory parking. It expressly excludes adult entertainment, firearms sales, pawnshops, and gasoline service stations from retail uses, and Section 9.2 prohibits industrial and manufacturing uses. Thus the lease includes permitted use restrictions consistent with the term sheet.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires minimum 8,000 SF publicly accessible open space
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.5(a) of the lease expressly provides that the Project shall include not less than 8,000 square feet of publicly accessible open space on the waterfront (eastern) side of the Premises, maintained by Tenant at its sole cost and connected to the existing public pedestrian promenade. This satisfies the criterion exactly, with additional detail in Sections 9.5(b)-(e) regarding design approval, non-dedication, rules/hours, and indemnity.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes assignment/subletting provisions with ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes Article 11 governing assignment, subletting, and the Authority's right of first refusal. Section 11.5 grants the Authority a ROFR during the period ending September 30, 2045—i.e., the first 20 years from the October 1, 2025 Lease Commencement Date—for proposed Transfers of the Lease to non-Affiliates for consideration. Section 11.1 also requires consent for Transfers, and Section 11.3 defines permitted transfers. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes finished floor elevation requirement of at least 15 ft NAVD88
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.8 does not impose a requirement that the finished floor elevation be at least 15 feet NAVD88. It only states that Tenant "shall maintain the minimum finished floor elevation required by the Approvals and Applicable Law" and that Tenant "may elect" to construct the ground floor above 15 feet NAVD88 for resilience purposes. The 15-foot NAVD88 figure is therefore permissive, not mandatory. Elsewhere the lease references the FEMA Base Flood Elevation of 12 feet NAVD88 (Section 12.4, Exhibit I) as the regulatory datum, confirming that no 15-foot minimum requirement is imposed. Since the criterion requires an affirmative finished floor elevation requirement of at least 15 ft NAVD88, the output fails.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes default and remedies provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes comprehensive default and remedies provisions. Article 15 (Section 15.1) defines at least five Tenant Events of Default with specific notice/cure periods: failure to pay rent within 10 Business Days after notice; failure to perform non-monetary obligations within 30 days after notice (extendable if diligently pursued); uncured Milestone Failure (subject to the 180-day Milestone Cure Period and Leasehold Mortgagee cure periods); bankruptcy/insolvency events; and material misrepresentation not cured within 30 days. Article 14 (Section 14.1) defines Landlord Events of Default with cure periods, including failure to perform material obligations continuing 30 days after written notice and failure to pay amounts due within 30 days after demand. Remedies are set out in Sections 15.3–15.4 (Landlord remedies, damages measure, mitigation) and 14.3–14.4 (Tenant remedies, offset, termination after 120 days). Additional notice/cure mechanics for Leasehold Mortgagees appear in Section 10.3 (60/90/180 days). The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes indemnification provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains environmental and broker indemnities, but it does not include a general Tenant indemnification of the Authority for claims arising from Tenant's use and occupancy of the Premises. Section 5.8(b) is limited to environmental matters, remediation, construction/operation in violation of Environmental Requirements, and hazardous materials introduced by Tenant; it does not cover ordinary use-and-occupancy claims such as personal injury or property damage on the Premises. Therefore, the specific required indemnification provision is missing.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes casualty and condemnation provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 13 of the lease is dedicated to 'CASUALTY AND CONDEMNATION.' It includes Section 13.1 requiring Tenant to restore the Improvements after a Casualty using insurance proceeds, Section 13.2 rent abatement, Section 13.3 termination rights on casualty, and Sections 13.4–13.7 addressing condemnation, including allocation of the condemnation award between Landlord (fee interest) and Tenant (leasehold, Improvements, trade fixtures, relocation, business interruption), plus partial and temporary takings and mortgagee rights. Both casualty and condemnation provisions are clearly present.

criteria_results.title: Memo includes at least three negotiation recommendations identifying counterparty and specific lease provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo contains numerous negotiation recommendations, each tied to a specific counterparty (the Authority/Authority's counsel/Landlord) and specific lease provisions. Examples: Issue 2 fallback on the reverter — 'If the Authority will not accept a "greater of" test, accept Net Hard Costs alone...' tied to Section 7.7; Issue 4 — 'If the Authority insists that the abatement begin on the Lease Commencement Date... trade it for a corresponding reduction elsewhere' tied to Section 6.3; Issue 5 — 'If the Authority refuses full lockstep indexing, a partial index is still far better than none' tied to Section 4.2; Issue 8 — 'If the Authority will not amend the recorded declaration, obtain a recorded subordination' tied to Section 11.6; Issue 9/10/11/12 fallbacks similarly tied to Sections 5.4, 9.6(b), 7.4, and 8.3. Part VII also lists 16 deliberate departures with priorities and Board-action notes, and Part X schedules a negotiating session with Authority counsel on Article 7 and Section 4.2. This far exceeds the three-recommendation threshold.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes lender's right to foreclose/assign to qualified transferee
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.6 expressly grants each Leasehold Mortgagee the unconditional right to foreclose (judicially or by power of sale), accept a deed in lieu, and assign the Lease to a transferee following foreclosure or deed-in-lieu without Landlord's prior consent. Section 10.6(b) requires such transferee to meet reasonable financial and experience qualifications substantially similar to those required of Tenant as of the Effective Date, with Landlord obligated not to unreasonably withhold recognition and to execute estoppels/consents. Section 10.6(c) further confirms such transfers are not Transfers under Article 11, do not trigger the ROFR, and require no fee. Article 11.6(a) and the SNDA provisions (Exhibit E) reinforce these lender protections. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies the construction loan from Bayside Federal
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly identifies Bayside Federal Lending Corp. as the construction lender. Recital E states the Project will be financed in part with a construction loan from Bayside secured by a first-priority leasehold mortgage; Bayside is defined as a Leasehold Mortgagee and Qualified Mortgagee, and Section 17.1(f) references an ALTA Leasehold Loan Policy in the amount of $285,000,000 insuring the first-priority lien of the Leasehold Mortgage, matching the approximate construction financing amount. Article 10 grants extensive lender protections, and a signature acknowledgment block for Bayside is included. The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Tenant's obligation to comply with affordable housing covenant
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.4(a) expressly requires that not less than fifteen percent (15%) of residential dwelling units be designated as Affordable Units available to households earning at or below eighty percent (80%) of Area Median Income 'for the duration of the Term,' documented in a recorded declaration consistent with the Affordable Housing Restrictive Covenant. This is reinforced by Section 9.4(b)-(g) (calculation, AMI determination, distribution, marketing/verification, enforcement, and a bar on Landlord reducing the requirement) and by Exhibit G (Affordable Housing Requirements), which repeats the 15%/80% AMI requirement, term duration, and related obligations. The lease thus contains the required affordable housing covenant obligation.

criteria_results.title: Both deliverable files are produced
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced two distinct deliverables: (1) a complete Ground Lease Agreement document (ground-lease-agreement.docx) with all articles, sections, exhibits, and signature blocks, and (2) a separate, substantial cover memorandum/drafting issues memo (drafting-issues-memo.docx) analyzing issues, conflicts, and gaps in the transaction record. Both required deliverable files are present and complete, satisfying the criterion.
